content_voiceover: This slide lays out the full ABO biosynthetic pathway step by step, and it's worth memorizing the sequence exactly. You start with a precursor structure. Alpha-L-fucosyltransferase, the product of the H gene, adds fucose to build the H antigen. From there, the ABO gene takes over, branching in two directions. Alpha-galactosyltransferase, the B-transferase, adds galactose onto the H antigen to build the B antigen. Alpha-N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase, the A-transferase, adds galactosamine onto the H antigen to build the A antigen. Notice both A and B transferases require the H antigen as their substrate, they cannot act on the precursor directly. That's why H gene failure is so consequential, if fucosyltransferase never runs, there's no H antigen, and downstream A and B transferases have nothing to modify, regardless of what ABO genotype the person carries. This produces the Bombay, or parabombay, phenotype. One naming note for boards, the old name Bombay has been officially updated to Mumbai, reflecting the city's renaming, so you may see either term used interchangeably in newer references.
keypoints: Pathway: precursor -> H antigen (fucosyltransferase, H gene) -> A or B antigen
B-transferase (alpha-galactosyltransferase) adds galactose to H antigen
A-transferase (alpha-N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase) adds galactosamine to H antigen
H gene failure blocks the whole pathway -> Bombay/parabombay phenotype regardless of ABO genotype
Naming update: Bombay is now called Mumbai phenotype
keypoint_voiceover: Memorize this pathway in order. Precursor becomes H antigen through fucosyltransferase, the H gene product. Then the ABO gene branches, alpha-galactosyltransferase adds galactose to make B antigen, alpha-N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase adds galactosamine to make A antigen. Both depend entirely on H antigen as substrate, so if the H gene fails, no H antigen forms, and A and B transferases have nothing to act on, producing the Bombay, now renamed Mumbai, phenotype, no matter what ABO genes are present.
